tracks.title: Capability as one object
tracks.text: Lesson three — toolkits. Tools that teach themselves. A toolkit is a capability you install into the ecosystem. A real program, compiled to WebAssembly… wrapped in a readable manual that teaches people and agents alike how to use it. [curious] This lesson is about why that bundle is one thing and not three… and why this layer is the frontier.

tracks.title: A million lock files
tracks.text: A million lock files — that's the tooling story today. Watch what happens when you give an agent tools. This framework has its own plugin format. That one wants tool servers, with their own protocol. The actual capabilities live in npm packages… pip packages… system binaries. Each arriving with its own dependency tree, its own lock file, its own security story to audit. [sighs] Set up a second agent stack… and none of it transfers. You end up managing tools… for your tools. The instinct is to fix this with one more format. [chuckles] Which is how we got this many formats. The actual fix is structural. A tool needs three things to be useful. First — code that runs. Second — a place it can run safely. And third — an explanation of how to use it. Today, those are three different artifacts, maintained by three different ecosystems. [excited] A toolkit is what you get when they're one object.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition, set like a dictionary entry. Toolkit… noun. A capability installed into the ecosystem. A real program compiled to WebAssembly… wrapped in a readable manual that teaches people and agents how to use it. Sandboxed… signed… and shareable as one unit. Think of a tradesman's toolbox. The tools… the safety case they lock into… and the dog-eared manual in the lid. Picked up and carried as one thing. [chuckles] Nobody hands you a drill bit, a warehouse address, and a PDF… in three separate shipments.

tracks.title: Three layers
tracks.text: Three layers. Picture them as three hexagons, stacked like a totem — manual on top, wasm in the middle, sandbox at the base. One signed unit… manual, muscle, floor. The first layer is the surface — the manual. A small tree of plain-text documents describing what the tool does, when to reach for it, and how each command works… with worked examples. A person reads it like documentation. An agent reads it like a skill. Same words — both audiences. Write the manual once, and you've onboarded every human and every agent that will ever meet the tool. The second layer is the muscle — a real program. An actual CLI… not a description of one. Written in whatever language suits the job, compiled to WebAssembly. And existing tools matter here. A battle-tested C library becomes a toolkit by compilation… not reinvention. [excited] And the third layer is the floor — the sandbox. Toolkits run inside the Nexus, with the capabilities they're granted and nothing more. Installing a tool used to mean trusting its author with your machine. Installing a toolkit means trusting it with exactly what you handed it.

tracks.title: The manual is the interface
tracks.text: The manual is the interface — and here's the design decision that makes toolkits feel different. Agents turn out to work best, not with a hundred bespoke integrations… but with one general tool — a shell — and useful programs on the path. That's how people work at a terminal too. It's why the CLI never died. So a toolkit doesn't add a new protocol to your agent. It puts a command on the path… and the manual next to it. And because the manual is structured text rather than free-form prose, it does double duty. It documents the tool… and it's parseable enough to act as the tool's API. [excited] The documentation can't drift away from the tool… because the documentation is how the tool is reached. If you've used skill files with a coding agent — this is that idea, taken to its conclusion. The skill, the binary it teaches, and the sandbox it runs in… shipped as one signed object.

tracks.title: Isn't this just an MCP server?
tracks.text: [curious] Isn't this just an MCP server? Or a plugin… or an npm package? Line them up on a scorecard, with four tests. Does the code run. Is there a safe place to run it. Does it teach its own use. And does it carry to any host. An npm package gives you code that runs — on your machine, at your risk… with a readme, maybe. An MCP server gives you code behind a protocol — but a schema isn't guidance, and you bring your own sandbox. A platform plugin runs in the host's sandbox — and it's locked to that host. Each one passes a test or two, and leaves you to source the rest. The toolkit row is the only one that says yes four times. The code runs… the wasm sandbox bounds it… the manual is the surface… on any Nexus, in any workbook. None of those other things are bad ideas. Toolkits happily wrap existing CLIs rather than compete with them. [excited] The claim isn't better protocol. It's that code, sandbox, and manual were never supposed to be three separate supply chains.

tracks.title: Why WebAssembly?
tracks.text: Why WebAssembly? This is a depth rung — the engineering bet under the whole layer. Because untrusted code is no longer the exception… it's the medium. Tools you didn't write… packages with install scripts… code an agent generated thirty seconds ago. All of it wants to run. And an install script is just untrusted code you execute with your own permissions. WebAssembly is the only runtime that was born for this. Designed from day one to run a stranger's code fast, in a sealed box, on any hardware. Browsers have been stress-testing that box with the entire internet… for years. [excited] And the deeper bet — the crux of the whole system — is migrating the languages of the internet into that box. The ecosystem carries compilers for C, Rust, Zig, Go, and JavaScript… that have themselves been compiled to WebAssembly. Source goes in… the sandboxed compiler chews… a signed toolkit comes out. And at no point did anything untrusted execute natively on the host. And one bonus falls out for free. WebAssembly runs in browsers. The same compiled tool a Nexus runs server-side can ride along inside a workbook. One compilation target… every venue.

tracks.title: Toolkits compose
tracks.text: Toolkits compose — single tools are just the start. Because every toolkit shares the same shape — manual, muscle, floor — they stack without negotiation. Three ways, in rising order. First: tool systems. Toolkits bundled toward a job… a research rig, a publishing pipeline, a media bench. Second: agents. An agent definition is a toolkit-shaped thing — the manual describes who the agent is… the tools are what it reaches for. And third: workflows. Plans written in the same readable layer… closer to a project board than a script. [excited] And the street runs both ways. Build something useful inside a workbook — a parser, a chart kit, a scraper — and one command promotes it into a toolkit the next workbook can pick up. The parts bin is fed by the things people actually make. [chuckles] Which is the only way a parts bin ever gets good.

tracks.title: The honest frontier
tracks.text: Honesty section — the honest frontier. And this lesson owes you a bigger one than the others. Toolkits are the youngest part of the ecosystem. The unit is stable. The engine is built on forty-year-old, miracle-grade infrastructure. The parts bin is early. Real… working… growing… and small. Browse it at a terminal and you can hear the shape of it. List the toolkits, and five come back ready — glyphs, for logos and icons as SVG… ffmpeg, for media… a video maker… a deep-research browser… a deploy tool. Ask about glyphs, and the manual itself answers — three skills: curate, integrate, resolve. Build it — it compiles to wasm, sandboxed and signed. Push one of your own, and it ships onto the engine… where any workbook can pick it up. The catalog grows one conversion at a time. Most software crosses cleanly. Some puts up a fight — but each fight won is permanent. [excited] And that's also the invitation. If the workbook lesson convinced you, and the Nexus lesson convinced you — this layer is where a contribution actually lands. Convert one tool you love… write the manual you wish it had… and you've added a part to everyone's bin.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire — the questions people actually ask. [curious] What languages can a toolkit be written in? Anything that compiles to WebAssembly. C, Rust, Zig, Go, and JavaScript have first-class lanes today. Can I publish my own? Yes. Build it… sign it… share it. Why would I trust a stranger's toolkit? Two reasons, layered. The signature tells you who shipped it. And the sandbox bounds what it can do — regardless of who shipped it. Even a hostile toolkit holds only the capabilities you granted. [chuckles] Which is a stronger guarantee than any code review. Does a toolkit work offline, inside the file? Yes — browsers run WebAssembly, so tools can compute client-side, in the open file. And — I have a CLI I already love. Do I rewrite it? Ideally, no. You compile it. That's the whole point of the conversion path.

tracks.title: Wrapping up
tracks.text: So that's a toolkit. Code that runs… a floor it can't fall through… and a manual both species read. One signed object. [curious] Next… the grammar that holds every one of these pieces together. Org.
